finding: §4 conditions `by_severity` on the rows rather than the policy, and justifies that entirely by `--merge`'s inability to resolve the workflow. But this release has two sinks that DO resolve it — §7 row 3 makes an invalid stored value fail at `tp audit --record` and `--status`, and §2 stamps `clean` at record time under the resolved policy — and neither is priced as the home for the breakdown. The consequence is paid by the default path: `all` is the default, §2.1 argues in 2 of 2 measured cycles that it should stay the default, and under `all` every non-`PASS` row already blocks, so the breakdown feeds no decision an agent makes. Every project therefore parses a new key on every merged round holding a non-`PASS` row, and row 16 makes it survive `--compact` — the surface whose whole job is to strip what the agent does not need.
suggestion: Price the alternative in §4: emit `by_severity` from `--record`/`--status`, which resolve the policy and already walk the round's rows, leaving `--merge` unchanged. If it must stay on `--merge`, justify the `all`-path cost by a decision an agent makes under `all`, not by the sink's limitation, and let `--compact` strip it there.

finding: This round's repair gives one refusal message two incompatible audiences. The same refusal fires for an authoring error (remedy: edit the document, and §3 requires the message to name the two forms that pass) and for a unit that intends the relax (remedy: `tp escalate --decision audit-converge-on`). A unit that meant to relax reads a message stating that carrying `"audit_converge_on": "all"` makes the import pass, does exactly that, and silently reverts an operator-approved `blocking` — no escalation, no round-trip, no record. §7 row 14 pins only that the message names the two documents and that it avoids the command-field wording, so a message that never mentions the escalation path passes every assertion in the release.
suggestion: Make the message name all three exits with the condition that selects each, or split the refusal by what changed: name the two documents when the resolved-before value was already `blocking` (the uncovering/authoring case), and name escalation when the write itself introduces the literal. Add a §7 row pinning that the message names the escalation path.

finding: The accepted count is delivered as a numeral inside the prose `next_action` string, while §4 states that the same population's count is already emitted machine-readably and unconditionally as `role_streaks[].open` on both `--status` and `--record`. The release therefore asks an agent to regex a number out of English that it can already sum from a key it parses anyway. The two differ only on roleless rows, which §6.5 says `auditRoundOpenByRole` drops — 20 of them across 90 recorded rounds — so the new channel exists to carry a delta of at most those rows. Row 10 then freezes the prose channel as a contract by pinning the numeral in the string.
suggestion: Emit the count as a key beside `next_action` and leave `next_action` a directive; or attribute roleless rows in `auditRoundOpenByRole` so the count is derivable from `role_streaks[].open` and add nothing. If the numeral stays in the string, state why an agent should parse prose for a number tp can key.

finding: `by_severity` is emitted only when the round holds a non-`PASS` row, so its absence is ambiguous to the consuming agent: a clean round, or a tp older than v0.37.0. Disambiguating costs a version probe or a `by_status` cross-check on every merge — a round-trip paid on the common case to save a few bytes on the rounds that already carry the least output. It also inverts this codebase's own JSON convention that an empty collection serializes as an empty value rather than vanishing.
suggestion: Emit `by_severity` unconditionally, as `{}` on an all-`PASS` round, and change row 15's assertion accordingly; or state in §4 how a consumer distinguishes 'clean round' from 'unsupported binary' and add a row pinning that.

finding: §3 adds `audit-converge-on` to the closed, validated `--decision` enum, but this round's repair removed its only described producer. Every unattended refusal §3 walks through is now classified as something other than an escalation: the direct write and the write-`all`-then-`blocking` sequence are walk-arounds to refuse, and the uncovering import is 'an authoring error the unit fixes itself — not an escalation'. A unit that 'intends the relax' is asserted but never shown to be a reachable state under `tp run`, where §3 itself says the decompose unit regenerates the document each iteration rather than choosing a policy. §7 row 14 tests only that the enum accepts the value, not that anything produces it.
suggestion: Name the reachable unattended path that legitimately escalates this decision (and give it a §7 row), or drop the enum value and let the case stop under `other` until a producer exists. A closed-enum value with no producer is surface the operator can never observe.

finding: §6 makes the sweep the deliverable and the five-item list explicitly illustrative, but §7 pins only the five listed items (rows 18-21). Nothing checks the sweep, so its four-clause predicate over `skills/`, `README.md`, `internal/engine/` and `internal/cli/` doc comments is re-run by hand — by a reviewer, an implementer and every future round that re-reads the section — and produces no artifact anyone can diff. The spec supplies the cheap mechanization in its own text and declines to adopt it: `git grep review_converge_on -- skills/` is stated to have returned a sixth item in one command.
suggestion: Register the derivable half as a `workflow.checks` entry or a guard test — a grep-based inventory over the four trees asserting that every hit states a rule true under both values — and leave only the judgement half in task acceptance. Give §7 a row whose subject is the check itself, so the sweep has an observable.

finding: The one input the knob's decision needs — the previous cycle's severity mix — is served by a shell one-liner parked in `skills/tp/SKILL.md`, outside every tp surface the operator is already standing on, and §7 has no row for it, so it can rot without reddening anything. Meanwhile §4 computes exactly this breakdown per round on `--merge` and does not persist it. The release ships the number on the sink where it is discarded and sends the operator to grep for it at the moment the decision is made — and §2.1 states that moment is before round 1 is recorded, i.e. when the operator has the least state to work from.
suggestion: Have `tp audit --status` report the resolved cycle's severity mix; it already walks the round files, so the marginal cost is a counter, not a walk. If the one-liner stays, pin it with a check so it cannot drift, and say in §2.1 why a shell round-trip is cheaper than the walk `--status` performs anyway.

finding: §2 says `AuditNextAction` 'gains the count' and never says the boolean goes. `latestRoundHasFindings` is exactly `count > 0` under §2's own definition of the count (the latest recorded round's non-`PASS` rows), so the reading that keeps both makes every call site compute the same fact twice — and this repo enables `unparam`, so that reading does not merely waste bytes, it fails the quality gate. The stated justification, that 'the two facts the boolean folds together are now different questions', describes `clean` versus has-findings, which is not what the boolean carries; the boolean carries only has-findings.
suggestion: State the resulting signature literally — the boolean is replaced by the count — and make §7 row 10's subject the parameter list, so the mutant 'keep the boolean and pass `count > 0`' is visibly wrong rather than a defensible reading of the spec.

finding: Row 22 pins the ABSENCE of a divergence object for roleless open rows, and its own mutant column says the change it forbids is `spec/0.46.0.md` §8's decision to make. So this release writes a guard whose deletion is the successor's first task — which is precisely the cost §5 item 4 cites as the reason `nonblocking_open` stays deferred ('Four places pin its absence there by name'). The release names pinned absence as a blocker in one paragraph and adds a fifth pinned absence in another.
suggestion: Pin the cost in a form the successor can satisfy rather than must delete — assert that either the `unattributed_open` caveat is emitted or the roleless count is zero — or state in §6.5 that row 22 is expected to be removed by `spec/0.46.0.md` §8, so the next cycle does not read it as a standing contract.

finding: Taking §2.1's own conclusion as given, the release never draws the ledger its lens requires. Against a measured yield of zero cycles in which the field would have been set correctly, it adds: a workflow field with two literals, validation at two sinks, an unattended fence across three write paths plus a fourth writer to reason about, a new `--decision` enum value, a new `--merge` key that survives `--compact`, a changed `AuditNextAction` signature with two new string forms, five reversed shipped assertions, and 26 test rows. §1 asserts of the fence that 'This is what the release buys' without ever naming what it is bought against.
suggestion: State the expected yield and the evidence for it — a cycle whose remaining rows were all advisory at the point the streak would have closed — or cut the surface to the field plus its two consuming sinks, deferring the fence, the enum value and the `--merge` key until a project actually sets the field.

finding: The committed replay projection retains four fields — `status`, `severity`, `role`, `item_id` — across 3,046 rows for about 295 KiB, but the only row that consumes it is row 11, whose whole assertion is eight integers derived from per-round (clean-under-`blocking`, clean-under-`all`) verdicts. `role` and `item_id` have no consumer in §7: rows 17, 21 and 22 each name their own fixtures. Half the retained shape is committed for nobody, and it is committed permanently.
suggestion: Either name the rows that read `role` and `item_id` from the replay fixture, or narrow the projection to `status`, `severity` and the round ordinal. Cheaper still: commit the derived per-round verdict pairs (22 rounds x 2 booleans) with the derivation command beside them, and keep the row-level projection out of the tree.

finding: §2 defers the severity-aware streak question with 'Making the streak surfaces severity-aware is the role-scoping question §5 defers'. §5 item 1 opens by denying exactly that framing: 'That is role scoping, not severity scoping, and severity parity does not close it.' A reader following the pointer lands on a Non-Goal that disclaims the topic and must pay a second hop to `spec/0.46.0.md` §8 to find the owner — which §7's closing paragraph names directly, so the release already knows the short path.
suggestion: Point §2 at `spec/0.46.0.md` §8 the way §7's closing paragraph does and drop the 'role-scoping question' label, or add a Non-Goal for the severity-aware streak question distinct from item 1.

finding: Three mutant cells are stated over internal identifiers whose existence and shape can only be established against code: `hoistedFields` (row 4), `engine.ResolveWorkflowLayers` (row 2) and `refuseUnattendedCommandField` (row 14); §3 adds `auditRoundOpenByRole`, `AuditRowIsPass` and `IsLegacyRound`. Each pins mechanism that a task's acceptance should own, and each is a citation a rename silently falsifies while the spec keeps reading correctly — the failure mode the file's own header says forensics have.
suggestion: State the mutants behaviourally — a hoist that omits the field; a resolver that consults a layer beyond the two named; a refusal reusing wording written for command fields — and move the identifiers into task acceptance, where they are re-derived from the tree and checked by running.

finding: The header states this file is decisions and that forensics belong in task acceptance, then three passages narrate the drafting rather than the decision: §2's seven lines on what 'an earlier draft wrote' and the word `surviving` being deleted 'for imprecision'; §2's 'two earlier drafts left it to be inferred and both inferred it wrong'; and §6's 'The count has been one, two, three and five, and each number was falsified by the next round'. None states a rule an implementer follows, and all three are re-read by every role every round and by the decomposer.
suggestion: Keep the rule each passage arrived at — the predicate is over non-`PASS` rows; an unrecognised severity blocks; the sweep rather than a count is the deliverable — and move the drafting history to a candidates file, as `spec/0.35.0-candidates.md` already does for its cycle.

finding: §7's row identifiers run 9, 9b, 10, 11, 12, 13, 13b, 13d, 13c, 14 — `13d` is printed before `13c`, and the suffixes encode this spec's revision history rather than any ordering of the tests. A decomposer turning rows into tasks inherits an unsortable key and a table whose reading order contradicts its own labels; a later reader citing 'row 13c' cannot locate it by scanning.
suggestion: Renumber the rows sequentially now that the table is stable. The 'derives from' column already records which decision each row came from, so the suffixes carry no information that would be lost.
